title: Synthetic Quantum Systems (SQS)
text:
The Synthetic Quantum Systems (SQS) group at IIT Madras works in the interdisciplinary areas of quantum many-body physics, quantum simulation, condensed matter physics and quantum information science. Our projects combine analytical methods with large-scale numerical simulations, and many of them are motivated by experiments with synthetic quantum systems. More about our work can be found on the Research page.
We are always looking for motivated members. If you would like to join us, please see the openings below.

title: Research
text:
What happens when many quantum particles interact strongly? Electrons in a solid, atoms held in a crystal of laser light, or photons trapped in a cavity can then act collectively, in ways that no single particle could. They form new phases of matter, switch between them at sharp transitions, and build up intricate patterns of quantum entanglement. Understanding this collective quantum behavior is the goal of our research.
We approach it from several directions. We study how quantum matter organizes itself at low temperatures, with a particular interest in phase transitions that defy conventional wisdom and in topological phases. We explore lattice gauge theories, the language in which particle physicists describe the fundamental forces, in versions that can be built in the laboratory. We ask how matter changes when it interacts strongly with light trapped between two mirrors. We also follow quantum systems out of equilibrium, asking whether, how and how fast they forget where they started.
A common thread is quantum simulation. Ultracold atoms, Rydberg atoms, trapped ions and cavity experiments now let physicists assemble many-body systems almost to order, and watch them particle by particle. Our aim is to find the physics these platforms can reveal, and to provide the theory needed to recognize it. For this, we combine field-theoretical reasoning with large-scale tensor network simulations, and we borrow ideas from quantum information to characterize the states we find.

title: Research
text:
Current Research Topics

  
    Quantum Simulations with Synthetic Quantum Systems
    Atoms in optical lattices, Rydberg atoms and dipolar gases can be engineered to interact in ways rarely found in natural materials, for instance over long distances or through hopping that depends on the neighbors. We map out what such systems do for realistic experimental parameters, so that experiments know what to look for and how to recognize it.
    Key papers
    
      Phys. Rev. B 105, 155159 (2022)
      Phys. Rev. B 106, 035144 (2022)
      Rep. Prog. Phys. 88, 044501 (2025)
    
  
  
    Tensor Network Algorithms
    Tensor networks are the workhorse of our numerics. We use them for ground states, excitations and long-time dynamics, extend them to new territory such as gauge theories and light-matter systems, and test competing algorithms against each other to learn where each can be trusted. Our open-source library TenNetLib.jl grew out of this effort.
    Key papers
    
      Phys. Rev. B 101, 035148 (2020)
      PRX Quantum 4, 040317 (2023)
      Phys. Rev. B 110, 195114 (2024)
    
  
  
    Critical Phenomena
    At a phase transition, a system decides how to organize itself, and its behavior becomes universal. We are drawn to transitions that break the textbook rules: symmetries absent in the original model that emerge at long distances, or two incompatible kinds of order that meet at a single continuous transition. We study them in quantum chains, ladders and two-dimensional models.
    Key papers
    
      Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 256703 (2025)
      Phys. Rev. B 108, 075146 (2023)
      arXiv:2608.24248 (2026)
    
  
  
    Lattice Gauge Theories
    Gauge theories describe the fundamental forces of nature, from electromagnetism to the strong force that binds quarks. On a lattice, they become accessible to computers and to quantum simulators. We study how charges get confined, how gauge theories evolve after a sudden kick, and what changes when the matter is bosonic, as is natural with cold atoms.
    Key papers
    
      Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 180602 (2020)
      Phys. Rev. Lett. 128, 090601 (2022)
      Phys. Rev. B 114, 034205 (2026)
    
  
  
    Topological Order
    Some phases of matter cannot be told apart by any local measurement. Their identity is encoded globally and shows up in robust edge states, or in excitations that carry a fraction of an electron’s charge. We look for such phases in models that synthetic quantum systems can realize, from fractional quantum Hall states to quantum spin liquids.
    Key papers
    
      Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 196501 (2025)
      Phys. Rev. B 108, 075118 (2023)
      SciPost Phys. 12, 076 (2022)
    
  
  
    Cavity Control of Many-Body Systems
    Between two mirrors, light and matter can interact so strongly that they lose their separate identities. We study how this reshapes the phases of matter, which hybrid excitations of light and matter emerge, and how the light itself can tell us what is happening inside the material.
    Key papers
    
      Phys. Rev. X 15, 021027 (2025)
      SciPost Phys. 15, 113 (2023)
      Phys. Rev. B 106, 155113 (2022)
    
  
  
    Out-of-Equilibrium Phenomena
    Experiments with synthetic quantum systems naturally watch things move. We study how many-body systems respond when their parameters are changed suddenly or slowly, how phase transitions leave fingerprints in the dynamics, and how such dynamics might be put to work in quantum devices, for example to charge a quantum battery faster.
    Key papers
    
      Phys. Rev. B 103, L220302 (2021)
      Phys. Rev. B 101, 224304 (2020)
      Phys. Rev. A 104, 032207 (2021)
    
  
  
    Many-Body Localization and Disordered Systems
    Isolated quantum systems usually thermalize and forget their initial state, but disorder or strong fields can stop this from happening. Using simulations of large systems, we study when such localization sets in, how it differs between random and perfectly regular potentials, and how localized and thermal regions can live side by side.
    Key papers
    
      Phys. Rev. Research 2, 032045(R) (2020)
      Phys. Rev. Research 2, 032039(R) (2020)
      Phys. Rev. B 107, 144201 (2023)
    
  
  
    Quantum Information Theory
    Quantum information offers both questions and tools. We study entanglement and quantum magic, the ingredient a quantum computer needs to outperform classical ones, in many-body systems, and propose ways to measure them in experiments. Earlier work explored how quantum correlations survive noise and how they can be shared among many parties.
    Key papers
    
      Phys. Rev. A 109, L040401 (2024)
      Phys. Rev. A 91, 062119 (2015)
      Phys. Lett. A 382, 1709 (2018)

I am Titas Chanda, a theoretical physicist and an Assistant Professor in the Department of Physics at the Indian Institute of Technology Madras (IIT Madras). Here I lead the Synthetic Quantum Systems (SQS) research group, and I am also affiliated with the Center for Quantum Information, Communication and Computing (CQuICC).

  
    
    
      My journey
      From Siliguri to Chennai, by way of Kolkata, Prayagraj, Kraków, Trieste and Indore
    
    
  
  
    
    I grew up in Siliguri, a picturesque city in the foothills of the Himalayas in West Bengal, where I completed my schooling. I then moved to Kolkata to study physics at Jadavpur University, and afterwards joined the Harish-Chandra Research Institute (HRI) in Prayagraj for an Integrated M.Sc.-Ph.D. It was at HRI, under the supervision of Prof. Aditi Sen(De), that I began my research in quantum information theory.
    My academic journey then took me to Europe, first as a postdoctoral researcher at Jagiellonian University in Kraków, Poland, and later at the Abdus Salam International Centre for Theoretical Physics (ICTP) in Trieste, Italy. During these years, my research interests gradually expanded from quantum information theory to quantum many-body physics and condensed matter theory.
    In 2023, after nearly five years abroad, I answered the call of Swades and returned to India to join the Indian Institute of Technology Indore as an Assistant Professor. A year later, I moved to the Indian Institute of Technology Madras, where I now lead the Synthetic Quantum Systems (SQS) research group in the Department of Physics.
  

My research sits at the crossroads of condensed matter theory, quantum many-body physics, quantum information science and quantum simulation. At its heart is a simple question: how do interactions among many quantum particles give rise to collective behavior that no single particle shows on its own? To address it, I combine analytical tools from quantum field theory with large-scale numerical methods, in particular tensor networks, and with ideas from quantum information theory.
Much of our work is motivated by synthetic quantum systems, such as ultracold atoms in optical lattices, Rydberg atom arrays, trapped ions and cavity QED setups. In these platforms, exotic many-body Hamiltonians can be engineered and probed in the laboratory, which opens a new window onto fundamental questions in condensed matter physics and beyond.
More about my work can be found on the Research page.

We are delighted to welcome two new members to the SQS group.
Rajashri Parida joined us in September 2026 as a postdoctoral fellow, supported by an ANRF National Post-Doctoral Fellowship. She completed her undergraduate studies at Utkal University and her master’s at the Central University of Punjab, followed by a Ph.D. at NISER Bhubaneswar under the supervision of Dr. Tapan Mishra. Her research focuses on the collective properties of interacting quantum gases, with a particular interest in developing and applying tensor network methods to strongly correlated many-body systems. Outside research, she enjoys singing and chatting with her loved ones, and she is always keen to learn something new, in physics and beyond.
Aditya Sharma joined us in October 2026 as a Project Associate. He studied Mechanical Engineering at BITS Pilani, Goa Campus, with a minor in Physics. For his undergraduate thesis, he worked with tensor network methods for two-dimensional systems, in particular iPEPS and CTMRG. His interests span quantum many-body physics, tensor networks and quantum information. Outside research, he enjoys listening to music, singing and reading philosophy, and he is an animal lover who cares about animal welfare.
We are excited to have them on board and wish them every success at IIT Madras.




August 26, 2026



Sourabh’s first paper, Critical bifurcation and deconfined quantum criticality in an interacting cluster Ising chain, is now available as arXiv:2608.24248. As it happens, it is also my 50th arXiv entry.

  
    
    
  
  Near the critical point: the cluster SPT, disordered, x-FM and y-FM phases meet at the SU(2)2 WZNW point (red dot, c = 3/2). The red line separating the two ferromagnets is the deconfined critical line, with c = 1 and eight-vertex criticality. Extended view: the full phase diagram also contains z-AFM and floating phases.

The physics. The free-fermion cluster Ising chain hosts a critical point described by the SU(2) level-2 Wess-Zumino-Novikov-Witten theory, which can be viewed as a triplet of Majorana fermions with an exact O(3) symmetry. An interaction reduces this O(3) to its cyclic subgroup \(C_3\) and splits the triplet into a singlet and a doublet, whose gaps close independently. As a result, the critical point bifurcates into two critical lines. One of them separates two ferromagnets that, according to Landau theory, cannot be connected by a continuous transition. This deconfined critical line belongs to the eight-vertex universality class.




July 2026




We are delighted to welcome Tamal Kundu to the SQS group as a PhD student. Tamal completed his bachelor’s degree in physics at Jadavpur University in 2024 and his master’s degree at IIT Guwahati in 2026. Outside academics, he enjoys reading and playing football, and he is an avid supporter of FC Barcelona. We are excited to have him on board and wish him every success in his PhD journey at IIT Madras.




June 2026



Welcome to my new website! It replaces my earlier Google Sites page and gives me more flexibility. I will keep it updated with research highlights, publications, teaching material and news from the group.




April 2026




Sourabh and Neelanjana Dey, PhD students in the SQS group, attended the ICTP-IBM School on Quantum Computing and Simulation at the Abdus Salam International Centre for Theoretical Physics (ICTP) in Trieste, Italy, from April 20 to 30, 2026. Over two weeks, the school offered lecture courses by leading researchers on quantum computing, quantum simulation and related topics.




January 2026



2025 was an exciting year for our research, with publications in several leading journals, including Reports on Progress in Physics, Physical Review X and Physical Review Letters.

A review article in Reports on Progress in Physics surveys recent theoretical and experimental advances in non-standard Bose-Hubbard models, with particular emphasis on long-range interactions and quantum simulation with ultracold atoms.
A paper in Physical Review X develops a theoretical framework for fractional quantum Hall states coupled to quantum light, revealing cavity-induced topological phenomena such as graviton-polaritons and light-matter entanglement.
A paper in Physical Review Letters demonstrates that chiral graviton modes survive in lattice fractional quantum Hall systems, opening a realistic route to observing them in quantum simulation experiments.
Another paper in Physical Review Letters uncovers emergent phases and unconventional critical phenomena in frustrated clock models, revealing a new mechanism by which forbidden discrete symmetries emerge at long wavelengths.

October 2026




  Rajashri

Rajashri Parida joined us in September 2026 as a postdoctoral fellow, supported by an ANRF National Post-Doctoral Fellowship. She completed her undergraduate studies at Utkal University and her master’s at the Central University of Punjab, followed by a Ph.D. at NISER Bhubaneswar under the supervision of Dr. Tapan Mishra. Her research focuses on the collective properties of interacting quantum gases, with a particular interest in developing and applying tensor network methods to strongly correlated many-body systems. Outside research, she enjoys singing and chatting with her loved ones, and she is always keen to learn something new, in physics and beyond.
Aditya Sharma joined us in October 2026 as a Project Associate. He studied Mechanical Engineering at BITS Pilani, Goa Campus, with a minor in Physics. For his undergraduate thesis, he worked with tensor network methods for two-dimensional systems, in particular iPEPS and CTMRG. His interests span quantum many-body physics, tensor networks and quantum information. Outside research, he enjoys listening to music, singing and reading philosophy, and he is an animal lover who cares about animal welfare.
We are excited to have them on board and wish them every success at IIT Madras.




August 26, 2026



Sourabh’s first paper, Critical bifurcation and deconfined quantum criticality in an interacting cluster Ising chain, is now available as arXiv:2608.24248. As it happens, it is also my 50th arXiv entry.

  
    
    
  
  Near the critical point: the cluster SPT, disordered, x-FM and y-FM phases meet at the SU(2)2 WZNW point (red dot, c = 3/2). The red line separating the two ferromagnets is the deconfined critical line, with c = 1 and eight-vertex criticality. Extended view: the full phase diagram also contains z-AFM and floating phases.

The physics. The free-fermion cluster Ising chain hosts a critical point described by the SU(2) level-2 Wess-Zumino-Novikov-Witten theory, which can be viewed as a triplet of Majorana fermions with an exact O(3) symmetry. An interaction reduces this O(3) to its cyclic subgroup \(C_3\) and splits the triplet into a singlet and a doublet, whose gaps close independently. As a result, the critical point bifurcates into two critical lines. One of them separates two ferromagnets that, according to Landau theory, cannot be connected by a continuous transition. This deconfined critical line belongs to the eight-vertex universality class.

Sourabh and Neelanjana Dey, PhD students in the SQS group, attended the ICTP-IBM School on Quantum Computing and Simulation at the Abdus Salam International Centre for Theoretical Physics (ICTP) in Trieste, Italy, from April 20 to 30, 2026. Over two weeks, the school offered lecture courses by leading researchers on quantum computing, quantum simulation and related topics.




January 2026



2025 was an exciting year for our research, with publications in several leading journals, including Reports on Progress in Physics, Physical Review X and Physical Review Letters.

A review article in Reports on Progress in Physics surveys recent theoretical and experimental advances in non-standard Bose-Hubbard models, with particular emphasis on long-range interactions and quantum simulation with ultracold atoms.
A paper in Physical Review X develops a theoretical framework for fractional quantum Hall states coupled to quantum light, revealing cavity-induced topological phenomena such as graviton-polaritons and light-matter entanglement.
A paper in Physical Review Letters demonstrates that chiral graviton modes survive in lattice fractional quantum Hall systems, opening a realistic route to observing them in quantum simulation experiments.
Another paper in Physical Review Letters uncovers emergent phases and unconventional critical phenomena in frustrated clock models, revealing a new mechanism by which forbidden discrete symmetries emerge at long wavelengths.
